title: Fair work
hook: Jewish law protects both workers and employers

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was genevat da'at, stealing minds. Did you find the place you were tempted to mislead, and say it plain? Today, the honesty of a day's work, on both sides. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.

Porters are carrying wine for a man named Rabbah bar bar Chanan. Somewhere along the way, they drop a barrel, and it breaks. Wine all over the road. So he takes their cloaks, as payment for the loss. They go to the teacher Rav and complain. Rav tells him: give them back their cloaks. He does. Then the porters say: we're poor, we've worked all day, we're hungry, and we have nothing. And Rav tells him: go, pay them their wages. Today, what the Torah and the rabbis ask of the one who hires, and of the one who's hired.
screen: `A BROKEN BARREL.` → `GIVE BACK THEIR CLOAKS.` → `NOW PAY THEM.`

segments.voice: Turn fair work four ways. First, the clock. Leviticus says: "the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning." Deuteronomy adds that a day worker is paid before the sun goes down, "for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it." The Torah notices that someone is counting the hours until payday, and that the waiting itself is a weight. Second, beyond the letter. When Rabbah bar bar Chanan asks Rav whether that's really the law, Rav answers with a verse from Proverbs: "That thou mayest walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous." Commentators on this passage in tractate Bava Metzia read it as going beyond what strict law requires, because these were poor men who'd worked all day. Third, the worker's freedom. The same tractate records a teaching that a worker may stop in the middle of the day. The reason given is a verse: the children of Israel are God's servants, and the rabbis read it to mean they are not meant to be servants of servants. Work is an agreement, not a chain. Fourth, the other side. Jewish law also protects the one who hires. Maimonides writes that a worker must work with all their strength, and he points to Jacob, who told his wives he had served their father with all his power. Loafing on someone else's time is a kind of theft too. So fair work runs both ways: pay on time and with heart; work honestly and with strength.
screen: `PAID BEFORE THE SUN GOES DOWN.` · `THE WAY OF GOOD MEN.` · `NOT SERVANTS OF SERVANTS.` · `WORK WITH ALL YOUR STRENGTH.` · then, large: `FAIR WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat one worker fairly today. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people whose work touches your day: a cashier, a delivery driver, a cleaner, a colleague, someone you employ, or you yourself on the clock. Pick one. Ask what fairness looks like there. Maybe it's paying promptly, or tipping well. Maybe it's thanking someone by name. Maybe it's giving your own work your full strength for one honest hour. Choose one act, small enough to do today. Hold it until it's clear. The bell holds the time.
Fair work: wages paid on time, beyond the letter when needed, and honest effort given in return. Today's word.
Your line: fair work. Today, do your one act for the worker you chose before the sun goes down. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Jewish law codes devote whole sections to the duties of employers and workers, and some Jewish communities and organizations draw on these teachings in their own hiring and in public debates about labor.

pairs: give back the cloaks, pay the wages

myth: the Torah lets an employer pay a day worker whenever it's convenient
Leviticus and Deuteronomy say a day worker is paid before the sun goes down.
in the porters' story, Rav tells the employer to pay them even after the barrel broke
he cites Proverbs: walk in the way of good men.
Jewish law only protects workers, not employers
Maimonides says a worker must work with all their strength, pointing to Jacob.

fork.setup: you're Rabbah bar bar Chanan. your porters broke a barrel of your wine. you've already given back their cloaks. they say they're hungry and have nothing. what does Rav tell you?
options: you're even now; they owe you nothing more.
make them work off the loss tomorrow.
fork.reveal: Rav tells him to pay their wages too, citing Proverbs: walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous.

trapdoor: what you thought: fair work means following the labor rules.
what it means: paying on time with an eye on the worker's need, and giving honest effort in return.
what a scholar hears: Bava Metzia 83a, the porters and Proverbs 2:20; Bava Metzia 10a, servants not of servants; Maimonides, Laws of Hiring, on Jacob's full strength.

notes: Bava Metzia 83a: the porters' story (Rabbah bar bar Chanan, broken barrel, cloaks, Rav, Proverbs 2:20) is retold; confirm details, including that the Talmud frames it as beyond strict law (lifnim mi-shurat ha-din).
Bava Metzia 10a: the worker may withdraw mid-day, from Leviticus 25:55, 'My servants, not servants of servants' — paraphrased; confirm.
Mishneh Torah, Hiring 13:7: the worker's duty to work with full strength, citing Jacob (Genesis 31:6); confirm section number.
Leviticus 19:13, Deuteronomy 24:15 and Proverbs 2:20 quoted from KJV; confirm wording.
Original set to null: no single Hebrew term carries this day's word.

Editor: fixed the hook's grammar (the Talmud names one broken barrel); the 'beyond strict law' reading is now attributed to commentators, since the Gemara itself has Rav answer 'yes' when asked if it is the law.
